title: Mosaic: A Benchmark Suite for Differentiable Physics Solvers
claim: Heterogeneous components are wrapped behind one uniform interface, so they can be compared on shared tasks and scored in one table.
layout: 4 columns, left-to-right with arrows, stacked backends, results table at right
description: Four labeled columns read left to right, joined by arrows. The first column, 'Solver backends', is a stack of slate-gray boxes naming solvers (PhiFlow, XLB, PICT, FEniCS, INS.jl, OpenFOAM, deal.II), with a faded '...' box at the bottom. An arrow leads to a dark 'Tesseract' box in the 'Standardized interface' column. It shows monospace signatures, apply(x) → y in blue and vjp(x, v) → g in red. Blue and red curved arrows lead from it to two flow-field heatmaps in the 'Benchmark tasks' column. The top heatmap is a forward solve with uniform blue inflow arrows around a circular obstacle. The bottom is an optimized inflow found via gradient, with red arrows of varying length. An arrow leads to the 'Evaluation results' table. Its rows are solvers and its columns are Fwd, Cost, Grad and Opt., filled with full, half and empty circle symbols for pass, partly and not applicable. The eye goes first to the colorful heatmaps.
caption: Overview of Mosaic. Diverse solvers are wrapped behind a uniform containerized interface, enabling cross-solver comparison on shared benchmark tasks involving different physical domains.
abstract: Differentiable partial differential equation (PDE) solvers underpin solver-in-the-loop MLtraining, gradient-based optimal control, and inverse problems, yet the practical cost of obtaining correct, usable gradients from a given solver on a given problem is largely undocumented. Integration effort, computational cost, memory, gradient accuracy, and numerical stability vary widely across solvers and are discoverable only by trial and error. We introduce Mosaic, an extensible benchmarking framework for differentiable PDE solvers that standardizes access to solver gradients. Each solver is packaged as a containerized component (Tesseract) exposing a uniform gradient API regardless of language or automatic differentiation (AD) strategy, enabling researchers to evaluate, compare, and build on non-trivial physical solvers. Our evaluation of 14 solvers across fluid dynamics, structural mechanics, and heat transfer demonstrates that the benchmark surfaces practically relevant differences: order-of-magnitude variation in computational cost and memory, alongside setup incompatibilities and instabilities that rule out solvers for specific tasks. Despite this variation, all solvers that produce gradients converge to similar optima on our tasks, indicating that the practical barriers are memory limits, numerical stability, and setup compatibility rather than gradient accuracy alone. Mosaic is open-source and available at github.com/pasteurlabs/mosaic.
